all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: degree of freedom
concepts.definition: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

defining_facts.text: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.
In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.
The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.

An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.

concepts.name: user group
concepts.definition: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

concepts.name: controlled experiment
concepts.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

defining_facts.text: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

concepts.name: experiment
concepts.definition: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

defining_facts.text: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

concepts.name: level
concepts.definition: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

defining_facts.text: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

concepts.definition: Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

never_defined.name: user characteristic
never_defined.definition: The user-centric approach, generally recommended for building interactive systems, is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, and it starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

never_defined.name: experimental study
never_defined.definition: In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

never_defined.name: confounding variable
never_defined.definition: In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.

never_defined.name: task sequence
never_defined.definition: To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied; statistically, these random or systematic variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.

never_defined.name: system implementation process
never_defined.definition: In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

never_defined.name: statistical significance
never_defined.definition: In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

never_defined.name: population
never_defined.definition: In empirical interface studies, the data are obtained from a sample of users rather than the actual population, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population, such as any user and any text-entry interface.

never_defined.definition: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

never_defined.name: mean text-entry speed
never_defined.definition: In comparing two text-entry interfaces, the analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between the means rather than the absolute values.

never_defined.definition: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.

never_defined.name: absolute difference
never_defined.definition: The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.

never_defined.definition: In a statistical significance test, such as a paired sample t-test, the p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.

never_defined.name: analysis of variance
never_defined.definition: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

never_defined.definition: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

never_defined.name: repeated measures analysis of variance
never_defined.definition: For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

never_defined.definition: For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.
